title: How Much Does an eCommerce Website Cost in Hong Kong?
description: What an online shop really costs to build in Hong Kong in 2026 — platforms, custom builds, payment gateways and the hidden costs most quotes leave out.
brief: Explain typical HK price bands: Shopify/WooCommerce template setup (HKD 15,000–60,000), custom storefront (HKD 80,000–250,000), and complex multi-channel/ERP-connected builds (HKD 250,000+).
List what drives cost: number of products, payment gateways (Stripe, PayMe, Octopus, AlipayHK), shipping rules, multilingual (EN/繁中), ERP/inventory integrations.
Mention hidden costs: domain, SSL, payment fees, hosting, maintenance, and that cheap builds hit these later.
Advise to budget with an outcome in mind and end with a soft CTA to we2Tech for an itemised quote.

title: App Development and the PDPO: What Hong Kong Businesses Must Know
description: How Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance applies to your app — data collection, consent, overseas transfers and the 2021 anti-doxxing amendments.
brief: Explain that the PDPO is Hong Kong's data privacy law and applies to any app collecting personal data from HK users.
Cover the key duties: clear privacy policy, consent before collection, purpose limitation, retention limits, and secure storage.
Mention data collected by common features (accounts, payments, location, analytics) triggers these duties.
Cover overseas data transfer guidance and the newer anti-doxxing provisions.
Advise that a responsible HK developer will bake these in from the start — and end with a soft CTA. Avoid legal advice wording; encourage consulting a lawyer for their specific case.

title: WordPress vs Custom Development: Which Is Right for Your Website?
description: WordPress or a custom-built site? We compare cost, flexibility, speed, security and maintenance so you can choose the right foundation in Hong Kong.
brief: Compare WordPress: fast launch, low cost, huge plugin ecosystem, easy content editing — but plugin bloat, slower performance ceilings, and custom logic can fight the platform.
Compare custom (React/Next.js): tailored UX, better speed/SEO control, scales with your product — but higher upfront cost and needs real development.
Give a decision rule: marketing/brochure site with frequent content changes → WordPress; portal/dashboard/eCommerce with unique flows → custom.
Mention that a hybrid (WordPress + custom front-end) is common.
End with a soft CTA to we2Tech for an unbiased recommendation.

title: How Long Does It Take to Build an App in Hong Kong?
description: Realistic timelines for mobile and web apps in 2026 — MVP in 6–12 weeks, full product in 3–6 months — and what actually changes the schedule.
brief: Give realistic bands consistent with the existing cost post: MVP 6–12 weeks, mid-range 3–5 months, complex enterprise 6+ months.
List timeline drivers: scope/feature count, design iterations, third-party integrations, client decision speed, testing, app-store review.
Explain why fixed milestones beat open-ended estimates and how parallel work (design while building backend) shortens timelines.
Warn against unrealistic promises and end with a soft CTA.

title: iOS First or Android First? How to Choose Your Launch Platform
description: Should your startup launch on iOS or Android first? Spending habits, reach and cost in Hong Kong — plus why cross-platform changes the answer.
brief: Explain the classic rule: iOS users spend more per user and are easier to reach first; Android has broader reach, especially across Asia including HK and mainland-adjacent users.
Add HK context: local market mix and how cross-platform frameworks (React Native/Flutter) often make the choice less critical.
Cover cost/time implications of building one platform first vs both via cross-platform.
End with a decision framework and soft CTA.

title: Fixed Price vs Hourly: Which App Development Billing Model Is Better?
description: Fixed-price and hourly billing both have traps. How to read quotes, avoid scope blowups, and choose the model that fits your project in Hong Kong.
brief: Explain fixed-price: predictable budget, good when scope is clear, but risk of scope wars unless milestones and change process are defined.
Explain hourly/retainer: flexible, good for evolving projects, but needs trust and clear reporting to avoid budget drift.
Explain what a good fixed-price quote contains: milestones, acceptance criteria, change-order process, QA and launch.
Recommend: well-scoped build → fixed milestones; ongoing product evolution → retainer.
End with soft CTA.

title: Progressive Web App vs Native App: What's Best for Your Business?
description: PWA or native app? Reach, offline, push notifications and cost compared — and when the 'best' answer is actually both.
brief: Explain PWA: installable via browser, no app-store review, cheaper, good reach — but weaker access to device features and inconsistent iOS support for some APIs.
Explain native: best performance, full device access, store presence, push — but costlier and requires store review.
Give decision rules: content/booking/catalog → PWA or web app; deep device usage/offline-critical/consumer product → native.
Mention hybrid reality and end with soft CTA.

title: Should You Build an App for Your Restaurant in Hong Kong?
description: Online ordering, reservations, loyalty and delivery — whether an app is worth it for HK restaurants, and the cheaper alternatives that work first.
brief: Cover the pain points: phone reservations, third-party delivery fees, loyalty without data.
Walk the ladder: booking website → online ordering web app → native app, and when each makes sense.
Give HK-specific angles: PayMe/Octopus/AlipayHK payments, openrice presence, multilingual menus (EN/繁中).
End with soft CTA for a free feasibility chat.
